entries.note: Literally love of wisdom; in the Middle Ages it also meant alchemy, occult knowledge or any speculative science, a breadth surviving in [[see:PhD]] and [[see:MPhil]].
Someone who likes the French, an example of the same love element found in [[same-root:philosophy]].
Shares the love element of [[same-root:philosophy]]; called the city of brotherly love, though the hosts say the name just means city of love.
Contains the same wisdom element as [[same-root:philosophy]]; the first half of [[same-root:sophomore]] is tied to it.
Doctor of philosophy, which keeps the broad old sense of [[see:philosophy]] as acquiring knowledge, not the narrow discipline.
Master of philosophy, which, like a [[see:PhD]], doesn't mean you studied philosophy, just that you pursued knowledge.
A second-year student, popularly explained as wise fool; the first half is from sophos, tied to [[from:sophism]] and second-year rhetoric, but the second isn't [[unrelated:moros]].
Literally sharp and dull, so itself an oxymoron; Rob wonders whether it inspired the fool reading of [[see:sophomore]].
First a craftsman or sage, then a paid teacher of rhetoric in fifth-century BCE Greece, starting with [[see:Protagoras]]; sophists became maligned for superficial, bad-faith arguments.
The first [[see:sophist]], an itinerant intellectual who trained elite youths in Athens for public life; associated with 'man is the measure of all things'.
Never wrote anything down; what we know of him comes from [[see:Plato]] and [[see:Xenophon]], who may have put words in his mouth.
The main source for [[see:Socrates]]; despite [[see:platonic love]], he wrote extensively about sexual love.
With [[see:Plato]], one of the writers through whom [[see:Socrates]] is known.
Questioning in which a premise is refuted by exceptions and reformulated, again and again, until reaching [[see:aporia]]: explaining yourself into a hole.
The final stage of the [[see:Socratic method]], when the questioning ends in puzzlement.
A famous [[see:sophist]] whose patterned, rhythmic style favoured sound over content, using [[see:isocolon]] and [[see:antithesis]]; the hosts debate how to pronounce his name.
A rhetorical device of successive clauses with equal length or structure, used by [[see:Gorgias]] and seen today in buy one get one.
Placing opposite ideas side by side for contrast, as in a line by [[see:Cicero]]; even AI writing picks it up: it's not this, it's that.
Not an attractive trait today because [[see:sophist]]s were accused of superficiality; related to [[same-root:sophomore]] and [[same-root:sophisticated]].
Originally not a compliment, meaning mixed with a foreign substance or impure, like a [[see:sophist]]'s convoluted logic; related to [[same-root:sophistry]] and [[same-root:sophomore]].
Named after [[from:Epicurus]]; holds that pleasure is what intrinsically matters, tempered by tranquillity and moderation, with [[see:ataraxia]] and [[see:aponia]] as highest goals.
Means pleasure; going further than [[see:Epicureanism]], its followers held that the only intrinsic good is pleasure, meaning positively enjoyable sensations, not just absence of pain.
With [[see:aponia]], one of the highest goals of [[see:Epicureanism]].
With [[see:ataraxia]], one of the highest goals of [[see:Epicureanism]].
From the Greek word for dog, related to [[same-root:hound]]; perhaps for the cynics' coarse, ascetic street life under [[see:Antisthenes]]'s credo, or for their meeting place, [[see:Kynosarges]].
Not the direct source of [[same-root?:cynicism]], which comes from the Greek for dog, though Rob suspects the two are related far enough back.
Related to the Greek word for dog behind [[same-root:cynicism]].
His credo that all one needs is virtue and strength of spirit, and that ill repute is good, may explain the dog-like lifestyle behind [[see:cynicism]].
A gymnasium near Athens where the cynics met, possibly the reason for the name [[see:cynicism]].
From the Greek for porch, after the painted porch at the Athens [[see:agora]] where [[see:Zeno]] lectured; its modern reserved, unemotional sense owes much to [[see:Marcus Aurelius]].
Founder of [[see:stoicism]], who lectured on a painted porch; the philosophy may not bear his name because followers thought him flawed.
The public space in Athens where [[see:Zeno]] lectured; the word means meeting place and gave [[gave:agoraphobia]].
From [[from:agora]], meeting place; essentially a fear of large spaces where many people could gather.
Roman emperor and the most famous stoic, whose Meditations on virtue and resisting temptation shaped modern ideas of being stoical.
What stoicism is ultimately about, applying facts rather than emotions; the hosts trace it to Greek [[from:logos]].
Meaning word, account or reason, and the rational order of the cosmos; its versatility explains the varied senses of [[gave:-ology]] words.
Seems to mean words or thoughts or study of something depending on the word, because Greek [[from:logos]] was so versatile.
Credibility or character in persuasion, from a Greek word meaning character, custom or disposition; associated with the [[see:Socratic method]] and rhetoric.
The appeal to emotion in persuasion, paired with [[see:ethos]].
From [[from:ta ethika]], the Greek title given to one of [[see:Aristotle]]'s treatises, a list of moral principles; not far from [[see:ethos]].
Came after [[see:Socrates]] and [[see:Plato]]; his treatises gave their names to [[see:ethics]] and [[see:metaphysics]], and he held that a thing's essence comes first.
From [[see:Aristotle]]'s [[from:Ta meta ta physika]], literally the things after the physics, written after his Physics; the after later shifted to beyond.
Now used to mean beyond, though in Greek it meant after, as in [[see:metaphysics]]; the prefix was discussed in a previous episode.
Friendly, nonsexual love, drawn somehow from the intellectual love of [[see:Plato]]'s [[see:Symposium]], though Plato wrote extensively about sexual love.
Plato's work in which [[see:Socrates]] argues about the highest form of love, the source of [[see:platonic love]].
A fraught term which, in the US, means something different from [[see:liberal]] and [[see:neoliberal]].
In the US a lefty insult, opposite to [[see:neoliberal]] beliefs, yet rooted in the idea that people should do as they want, so opposing sides share it.
Means free-market capitalism: deregulation, privatisation and reduced government, the opposite of what Americans call [[see:liberal]] beliefs.
Concerned with conserving and resisting change, though political conservatives aren't necessarily averse to it; etymologically basically identical to [[same-root:conservationism]].
Big-C Conservative means a member of Britain's Conservative Party; little-c means politically or socially conservative without belonging to it.
Especially regarding the environment, a more left-wing priority in the US, despite being etymologically almost identical to [[same-root:conservatism]].
A movement against monarchy, or in Ireland for joining the Republic; from Latin [[from:res publica]], affairs of the public, implying neither left nor right.
Related to [[see:existentialism]]; humans seek purpose while the universe offers silence, a permanent tension, associated with [[see:Albert Camus]] and [[see:The Myth of Sisyphus]].
Associated with [[see:absurdism]], meaning, very reductively, that everything we try to do is relatively pointless.
Sisyphus endlessly rolling a stone up a hill, the image associated with [[see:Albert Camus]]'s [[see:absurdism]].
From Latin ab-, off, and [[from:surdus]], deaf or non-verbal; either out of tune with reason, or, punningly, things literally [[see:unheard of]].
One theory for [[see:absurd]], since Latin surdus meant both unable to hear and unheard; Rob notes it applies a modern English expression.

From Latin [[from:nihil]], nothing; the view that existence lacks meaning, purpose or truth, harsher than [[see:absurdism]], largely from thinkers like [[see:Friedrich Heinrich Jacobi]] and [[see:Ivan Turgenev]].
A made-up word meaning to esteem something as worthless, built from a pile of terms meaning nothing, including the nihil of [[same-root:nihilism]].
One of the German and Russian thinkers Jess typically associates with [[see:nihilism]].
One of the thinkers Jess typically associates with [[see:nihilism]].
A reaction to the idea of divine human purpose: existence comes before essence, as [[see:Jean-Paul Sartre]] reversed [[see:Aristotle]]'s order.
From Latin meaning literally to stand out, almost like rising from the grave, or presenting yourself; related to [[same-root:stand]].
Related to [[same-root:exist]], literally to stand out.
Reversed [[see:Aristotle]]'s order for humans, who first exist and only then define themselves through choices and actions, the core of [[see:existentialism]].
Jess's pick: the philosophy where you choose whatever parts you want, which Rob calls the philosophy for the indecisive.
Rob's joke name for his personal philosophy, punned into rollerism: just rolling with it.
Rob's joke philosophy named after Jess, a counterpart to [[see:Robism]] that Rob says he could subscribe to.
Once spelled with Y, I or G, as [[from:ileve]]; be- was added as a more credible prefix, and [[see:relieve]] shaped its spelling; related to [[same-root:glauben]] and [[same-root:love]].
Looks unlike believe until you see that Old English wrote the Y sound with G; related to [[same-root:belief]].
Shares a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to care, desire or love with [[same-root:belief]] and [[same-root:libido]].
Shares a root with [[same-root:belief]] and [[same-root:love]], a link also made in the hosts' recent sexy episode.
Probably influenced the spelling of the ending of [[see:belief]], taking it further from its Germanic relatives.
A short philosophical statement attributable to a specific person, unlike a [[see:proverb]], with a sting in the tail; sometimes criticised as reductive.
Received wisdom with no specific author, unlike an [[see:aphorism]].

entries.term: the most difficult thing to find is the way to the signposts
entries.note: An [[see:aphorism]] by Polish aphorist [[see:Wiesław Brudziński]], which Rob likes as a philosophical statement.
The [[see:aphorism]] associated with [[see:René Descartes]]; its ergo is the same as English [[see:ergo]].
Means therefore; the same word as in [[see:cogito ergo sum]].
Quite the aphorist and a friend of the podcast for his quirky attempts to revamp the alphabet and English; author of [[see:he that lies down with dogs shall rise up with fleas]].

entries.term: he that lies down with dogs shall rise up with fleas
entries.note: A [[see:Benjamin Franklin]] aphorism about the company you keep.
Perhaps the ultimate poetic aphorist of recent centuries, writing whole poems that were aphorisms, like [[see:A wounded deer leaps highest]].
An [[see:Emily Dickinson]] poem, read by Rob, that keeps repeating that things shine brightest in adversity, like a wounded deer's last leap.
In [[see:A wounded deer leaps highest]], consumption, whose flush makes a cheek reddest where it hurts most.

entries.term: There is no frigate like a book
entries.note: Jess's favourite [[see:Emily Dickinson]] poem, about books as cheap treasure troves that carry us to faraway lands.
The first line of an [[see:Emily Dickinson]] poem that is itself an [[see:aphorism]].
The [[see:Hamlet]] character whose strings of sometimes contradictory aphorisms make him one of the most quoted, though [[see:William Shakespeare]] portrays him as full of empty words.
Whatever follows it is an [[see:aphorism]], reflecting how much Chinese wisdom comes in aphorisms.
A parody religion created in 2005 by [[see:Bobby Henderson]] around the [[see:Flying Spaghetti Monster]]; Rob jokes about being a staunch Pastafarian.
Deity of [[see:Pastafarianism]], an invisible being with a noodly appendage, invented to argue that if [[see:intelligent design]] counts as science, so should it.
Oregon State physics graduate whose open letter to the Kansas State Board of Education, protesting [[see:intelligent design]], introduced the [[see:Flying Spaghetti Monster]].
The view that life requires an intelligent cause or deity; its approval for Kansas classrooms prompted the [[see:Flying Spaghetti Monster]].
A predecessor of the much sillier [[see:Flying Spaghetti Monster]]: a claimed teapot orbiting Jupiter, where the burden of proof lies with whoever claims it.
A 1990s satirical goddess from the alt.atheism Usenet group, defined by contradictory invisibility and pinkness, parodying claims insulated from disproof.
A 1960s religion holding that order and disorder are human-made grids imposed on deeper chaos; it inspired [[see:The Illuminatus! Trilogy]].
Discordian-inspired satirical sci-fi adventure novels full of drugs, sex, magic and conspiracy theories, featuring [[see:Operation Mindfuck]] and [[see:fnord]].
In [[see:The Illuminatus! Trilogy]], attributing all national calamities, assassinations and conspiracies to the [[see:Illuminati]].
Blaming everything on them, which recurred through the 20th century, took off with [[see:Operation Mindfuck]].
In [[see:The Illuminatus! Trilogy]], a word schoolchildren are conditioned not to see consciously, so it triggers lifelong unease and confusion.
